comparison: Both evaluate the comparative performance claims (C5, C6, C38-C44) from Table 1. OpenEval finds the results SUPPORTED with caveats about true negative definitions, while peer reviewers find them UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating the FTMap comparison is invalid because FTMap identifies small molecule binding sites, not PPI hot spots. This represents a fundamental disagreement on the validity of the performance comparison.

Both evaluate the GCP60 case study (C83-C85, Figure 3). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED as an effective illustration of non-interface hot spot identification through indirect vdW contacts. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, with no challenges to this structural analysis example.

Both evaluate the CRADD example (C88-C94, Figure 4). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting the structural rationalization and clinical relevance demonstrate the method's ability to identify non-obvious hot spots. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, with no criticism of this case study.

Both address non-interface hot spot identification (C9, C47-C54, C80-C82). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as a key advantage over structure-based methods. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, not challenging the underlying data but invalidating the FTMap comparison that was used to support the claim about detecting non-interface residues. The disagreement centers on the validity of the comparative framework rather than the observations themselves.

Both evaluate the AlphaFold-Multimer comparison on unsolved complexes (C7, C56-C58). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting the complementary performance and appropriate exclusion of test complexes from training. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, with no challenges to this analysis or Table 2 results.

Both evaluate the experimental validation of eEF2 predictions (C8, C63-C67). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting the co-IP experiments clearly demonstrate loss of binding for F794A and functional assays show selective effects with proper statistical significance. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, with no criticism of the experimental data in Figure 2.

Both address methodological development claims (C3, C4, C32, C69, C104-C106). OpenEval finds the dataset construction and feature selection SUPPORTED with sufficient rigor and novel contribution. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the web server as potentially useful but challenging the novelty claim, stating the approach has been used for over a decade with dozens of prior papers. This represents disagreement on the novelty aspect while the technical execution is less contested.

OpenEval evaluates the gas-phase energy feature and thermodynamic rationalization (C72-C76) as SUPPORTED with plausible mechanistic explanation. Peer review R2 includes C72 in its evaluation but focuses on novelty concerns rather than specifically addressing the feature's validity. Limited direct comparison available.

OpenEval finds the expanded dataset construction (C71, C17, C28-C30) SUPPORTED, noting the broader definition is well-justified and the PPI-HotspotDB represents a significant resource. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these dataset construction claims.

OpenEval evaluates differences in true negative definitions (C45, C46, C70) as SUPPORTED but notes this complicates direct performance comparisons with SPOTONE. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methodological differences in negative class definitions.

OpenEval marks claims about predictions potentially being true hot spots for alternative partners (C86, C87) as UNCERTAIN, noting the speculation requires experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these claims.

OpenEval finds resource availability and computational performance claims (C10, C11, C107) SUPPORTED, noting they support reproducibility though computational time is relatively slow. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these practical implementation details.

OpenEval finds background and motivation claims (C1, C2, C12-C27, C68, C95) SUPPORTED as well-cited literature review establishing context. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these introductory claims.

OpenEval finds methodological advantages and distinctions (C33-C37, C77-C79, C96-C99) SUPPORTED, noting the advantages are demonstrated in results. Peer review R4 includes C79 but focuses on FTMap comparison validity rather than broadly evaluating these advantage claims. Limited direct comparison.

OpenEval finds the class imbalance observation (C110) SUPPORTED as an important consideration that makes the model's performance more impressive. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this dataset characteristic.
